title: Onion Next Frame
user: Solo pixel artists and tiny-game teams who need to check a drawing against both its previous and intended next animation frame without changing their main editor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A pixel-art editor user asks for a light table/onion skin that superimposes previous and future frames.
A Construct user specifically asks to show the next animation frame and says reordering frames is the current workaround.
An indie developer describes building a deliberately asset-light, text-and-32-colour game, where fast visual iteration matters.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 animation-editor requests name the same missing next-frame context; it is a frequent small interruption during frame-by-frame work.
current_workaround: Reorder frames, duplicate layers, lower opacity manually, or switch to a heavier animation package.
incumbents_and_gap: Aseprite, Krita, and Construct have editor-specific approaches; there is no tiny local cross-editor review surface for a numbered PNG sequence that intentionally previews both neighbours.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA: drag in a numbered PNG/GIF sequence, scrub current/previous/next with independently adjustable tint and opacity, and export a reference contact sheet. Non-goals: painting tools, asset hosting, collaboration, or AI interpolation.
success_measure: 40% of activated users import a second sequence within 14 days; median first preview is under 30 seconds.
monetization: free — local, no-account utility adoption is more valuable than charging a narrow preview feature.
constraints: All image decoding stays in-browser; respect GIF/video codec limits; do not claim a substitute for licensed editors.
why_distinct: It is a sequence-review instrument, not another raster editor or an AI animation generator.

title: Motion Graph Sketchpad
user: Web and game creators who want to prototype animation of arbitrary visual properties before committing to code or a full timeline editor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Graphite tracks a stalled animation roadmap, including animation time nodes plus play/pause/restart controls in a node graph.
A creator requests an animation pane because creating animations through Luau is cumbersome and gives creators poor UX.
An Ask HN post explicitly asks what art people would like to express, signalling continued demand for low-friction creative expression surfaces.

recurrence: Two separate creator platforms identify code-first property animation as a blocker; both requests are recent and product-specific.
current_workaround: Hand-write keyframes/scripts, use a full video editor, or build throwaway prototype controls.
incumbents_and_gap: Rive, After Effects, and Godot are powerful production tools. The gap is a disposable browser sketch that animates plain values and gives copyable CSS/JSON, without a project format or account.
smallest_useful_product: A local web canvas with 1–8 named numeric/colour properties, draggable keyframes, easing preview, and CSS/Web Animations/JSON export. Non-goals: character rigging, video rendering, team review, or generative content.
success_measure: At least 50% of sessions export a snippet, and 25% return to modify a saved local sketch within seven days.
monetization: free — embeddable exports create distribution; paid sharing would only be considered after repeat use.
constraints: Use only locally stored sketches by default; make exported code deterministic; clearly label browser support for timing functions.
why_distinct: The artifact is a transferable motion experiment, not a timeline editor or a no-code game engine.

title: Theory Playalong Sidecar
user: Beginning instrumentalists using a MIDI keyboard who want to see harmony and try ideas while a score or backing track continues playing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A MuseScore user asks to play an external MIDI keyboard during playback without inputting notes, specifically to try bass-line ideas in context.
A prospective electronic-music maker asks for the first practical steps because they cannot find a clear way to start.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 asks describe the same learning gap: hear context, play a note, and see why it works rather than stop playback or memorise labels.
current_workaround: Pause notation software, record ideas separately, or use a DAW and theory chart side by side.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore supports notation and apps such as Skoove teach preset lessons; neither is a lightweight, local sidecar that listens during arbitrary backing-track playback and visualises the current note against a selected key.
smallest_useful_product: Browser MIDI input plus local audio-file playback, a one-octave note/chord map, beat marker, and non-judgmental in-key/out-of-key history. Non-goals: score import, transcription, teaching marketplace, or generated accompaniment.
success_measure: 30% of users connect MIDI and complete three five-minute playalong sessions in their first week.
monetization: free — MIDI/browser compatibility and trust benefit from an instantly usable local tool.
constraints: Web MIDI availability varies by browser; audio files remain local; avoid health or pedagogical outcome claims.
why_distinct: It turns live, exploratory playing into visible harmonic context rather than grading a lesson or becoming a DAW.

title: Lesson Tab Card
user: Guitar teachers and self-teaching players who need to type a quick, legible chord/scale handout during a lesson and share it as a compact card.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A guitarist asks for a markup language to quickly type tablature and chord diagrams during lessons, prioritising speed over expressiveness.
A music-notation standards contributor requests strict JSON schemas so user-provided notation metadata can be validated rather than relying on prose documentation.

recurrence: A recent lesson-speed request and a separate notation-interchange request point to authoring friction and unreliable handoffs in music notation.
current_workaround: Draw diagrams by hand, fight a full notation editor, or paste plaintext tabs into chat/docs.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore, Guitar Pro, and Soundslice are deep notation products. They do not optimise for a 30-second, validated, shareable lesson card with chord grid, fingering, and one short tab line.
smallest_useful_product: Static web editor with a keyboard-first mini syntax, six-string chord/grid preview, validation, printable PNG/SVG, and shareable encoded URL. Non-goals: copyrighted song libraries, full-score layout, playback, or user accounts.
success_measure: Median time from blank card to exported diagram is below one minute; 20% of users create five cards in a month.
monetization: freemium — a free useful editor establishes a format; optional branded worksheet packs can fund it.
constraints: No bundled song/tab corpus; use original structural notation only; encode shared cards client-side and validate untrusted syntax.
why_distinct: It is deliberately a lesson handout format, not a replacement notation suite or a tab database.

title: MIDI Theory Lens
user: Music learners with a MIDI controller who want an immediate visual explanation of intervals, scales, and chord changes while they play their own notes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Web Platform DX project collects developer signals for Web MIDI, which enables browser access to MIDI input and output devices.
A music-theory creator describes needing visual relationships instead of a memorisation-first approach.

recurrence: Web MIDI remains an actively tracked web capability while a contemporary learner explicitly asks for visual theory understanding.
current_workaround: Keep a circle-of-fifths chart open, use a piano visualiser that ignores key context, or buy a course with fixed exercises.
incumbents_and_gap: Piano visualisers show pressed keys and theory courses prescribe curricula; the gap is an ad-free lens that responds to any improvised chord and makes one selected concept visible.
smallest_useful_product: A browser MIDI keyboard/fretboard view with a selected tonic, live interval labels, chord-quality guess, and a local replay trail. Non-goals: automatic composition, score transcription, user profiles, or course content.
success_measure: At least 35% of activated MIDI users change key/concept and record ten or more note events in a first session.
monetization: free — the thin, privacy-preserving theory lens should be accessible without subscription friction.
constraints: Feature-detect Web MIDI and offer an on-screen keyboard; do not store performance data remotely; chord guesses must be presented as suggestions.
why_distinct: It is an explanatory instrument for a learner's own improvisation, not a gamified course or an AI music generator.

title: Haptic Beat Relay
user: Friends and rhythm-game makers who want a simple way to turn a phone/controller into tactile beat cues and small responsive music games without an online service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks whether streaming music can change based on input from a phone and what app already does this.
A game developer requests DualSense adaptive triggers, advanced haptics, touchpad input, and motion sensors for more natural and immersive interaction.

recurrence: Two independent requests seek richer physical input/output around music or games, rather than ordinary tap-only interaction.
current_workaround: Use inaccessible commercial rhythm games, custom game-engine code, or audio-only metronomes with no tactile adaptation.
incumbents_and_gap: Rhythm games are closed experiences and game engines expose low-level APIs. The gap is a browser-ready, local cue relay for a short loop and one companion device.
smallest_useful_product: A host page loads a local beat loop; a second device joins with a six-character code and receives vibration cues, taps back on-beat, and shows a shared accuracy meter. Non-goals: music streaming, competitive matchmaking, payments, or social graph.
success_measure: 50% of started host sessions connect a second device and complete two 60-second rounds.
monetization: free — the frictionless party/learning loop needs no paywall; later creator packs could be one-time purchases.
constraints: Web Vibration and controller haptics are browser/device dependent; relay only ephemeral room state; no music catalogue or copyrighted loops included.
why_distinct: It supplies tactile, multi-device music interaction primitives rather than a content catalogue or a generic multiplayer framework.

title: Audio Reactive Scene
user: Indie site owners, streamers, and event makers who want a tasteful, controllable audio-reactive visual scene without recording visitors or embedding a heavy visualiser product.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker describes a free library of seasonal ambient visuals and background sounds intended to bring websites to life.
A music-player user asks for a Cava-style bar visualiser widget/plugin rather than existing VU or peak meters.

recurrence: Recent web-effects and media-player requests independently ask for more expressive audio-linked visuals.
current_workaround: Embed a generic waveform, use a CPU-heavy visualiser package, autoplay decorative effects, or commission a custom canvas sketch.
incumbents_and_gap: Cava, MilkDrop, and Vanta offer visualisers/effects, but a small embed that makes a restrained scene from the page's own opt-in audio with accessibility fallbacks is uncommon.
smallest_useful_product: A copyable web component with three local canvas scenes, Web Audio analyser input, motion-reduction mode, manual intensity controls, and static poster fallback. Non-goals: microphone analytics, cloud rendering, AI art, or audio hosting.
success_measure: 20% of configurator sessions copy an embed and 80% of those embeds load under 150 KB before optional assets.
monetization: free — an open embed maximises adoption; a paid scene pack can remain optional.
constraints: Audio/microphone activation must require user gesture; honour prefers-reduced-motion; ship only original visuals and sounds.
why_distinct: It is an accessible, privacy-first scene component, not an autoplaying effect library or a full music visualiser app.

title: Touch Canvas Drills
user: People learning to draw on an Android tablet or phone who want tiny, repeatable touch exercises that work offline and do not demand a desktop-first editor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Excalidraw's touch-device meta issue says the app is primarily optimised for desktop and lacks features modern tablet drawing users expect.
An Ask HN user seeks serious educational iPhone apps rather than lightweight, gamified options.

recurrence: A major web canvas project documents tablet friction while a separate mobile learner asks for more serious, useful phone learning experiences.
current_workaround: Use desktop-oriented whiteboards, buy a complex art app before learning basics, or follow passive video tutorials.
incumbents_and_gap: Procreate and Concepts are capable art apps; Excalidraw is a general whiteboard. The gap is an offline, pressure-agnostic drill pad that teaches touch control without pretending to be a full art package.
smallest_useful_product: Installable PWA with 20 timed line/curve/shape drills, a simple stroke replay, local progress calendar, left-handed layout, and export of a single drill image. Non-goals: social feeds, AI critique, cloud portfolios, or replacement drawing tools.
success_measure: 30% of users complete five drills across three different days; touch-to-first-stroke time is below ten seconds.
monetization: one-time — a small offline practice utility is a better fit for a transparent, low price than a creative subscription.
constraints: No biometric-style stroke profiling or uploaded artwork; test Safari/Android touch events; meet reduced-motion and contrast requirements.
why_distinct: It is deliberate-practice scaffolding for touch drawing, not a whiteboard clone or a generated-art app.

title: Game Logic Tiles
user: Puzzle-loving beginners who want to learn game-state and rule logic by changing small playable systems before being asked to learn a programming language or engine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A puzzle-game enthusiast asks for the best way to learn game logic programming and how experienced developers teach algorithmic thinking.
A Scratch user asks for configurable costume-editor key bindings, a small but direct example of learners needing tools to fit their own creative workflow.

recurrence: A newcomer explicitly seeks a way to learn game logic, while a current Scratch request demonstrates that creative learners quickly hit workflow limitations in fixed environments.
current_workaround: Follow tutorials verbatim, wrestle with a general-purpose engine, or use Scratch projects whose logic and UI are not organised as a teachable system.
incumbents_and_gap: Scratch, Godot, and Construct teach/build games but expose broad canvases. The gap is a collection of ten inspectable one-screen games where each rule is an editable tile with an immediate state diff.
smallest_useful_product: Static web app with grid puzzles, editable rule tiles (move, collide, collect, timer, score), a step button, and shareable challenge seeds. Non-goals: freeform programming, user-created asset marketplace, multiplayer, or LLM tutor.
success_measure: 50% of first-time users modify a rule and solve a changed level; 15% publish a challenge seed.
monetization: free — a durable, linkable learning toy benefits most from zero-account access.
constraints: Keep challenges age-appropriate; generate deterministic seeds; avoid tracking minors or requiring accounts.
why_distinct: It teaches the causal model of game rules through constrained experiments, not another visual-programming canvas.

title: Voice Riff Loop
user: New electronic-music makers who want to make a short rhythmic sketch with their own voice before buying instruments, plugins, or learning a DAW.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A music-tool maker presents voice-to-instrument and stem/isolation tools for creators, showing active interest in voice as music input.
A rhythm-game contributor requests audio streaming as an enhancement, citing the need to reduce memory pressure for more audio content.

recurrence: A current creator-facing voice-music launch and a separate rhythm-game audio request both point to demand for responsive, lightweight musical audio workflows.
current_workaround: Record voice notes, import and trim them in a DAW, use copyrighted sample packs, or abandon the first idea because setup is too large.
incumbents_and_gap: GarageBand, BandLab, and Ableton Note are capable but broad. The gap is a local, one-minute first sketch that captures, slices, quantises, and loops only the user's own voice without a content feed.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile-first PWA with one-tap record, manual trim/slice, four rhythm pads, fixed-tempo loop, WAV export, and a local project store. Non-goals: AI voice conversion, cloud upload, stem separation, social publishing, or licensed sounds.
success_measure: 25% of recording sessions produce an exported 15–60 second loop; median time from permission grant to audible loop is under two minutes.
monetization: one-time — the product is a focused instrument, not an ongoing media service.
constraints: Microphone use must be explicit and local-only; mobile browser latency varies; include no third-party samples or voice-model processing.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately constrained first-loop instrument, not a DAW, sample subscription, or AI music wrapper.

title: Voice Comfort Meter
user: Podcasters, singers, and public speakers who dislike their recorded voice and need a playful, private way to compare takes and understand simple recording changes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks why a recorded voice feels unfamiliar compared with one's internally heard voice and describes the discomfort directly.
A meta request collects user demand for clearer visual feedback while the app is recording, including a changing tray icon/visualiser.

recurrence: One asker describes the emotional recording problem while another product community asks for better live recording feedback.
current_workaround: Re-record repeatedly, inspect an intimidating DAW meter, or avoid recording and assume the mismatch is a technical failure.
incumbents_and_gap: Audacity, GarageBand, and podcast recorders expose professional meters; the gap is an encouraging take-comparison toy that makes gain, distance, and room noise understandable without diagnosis claims.
smallest_useful_product: Local web recorder with two 15-second takes, waveform/loudness/room-noise comparison, three plain-language setup prompts, and local WAV deletion/export controls. Non-goals: voice cloning, medical/hearing assessment, cloud storage, or automatic beautification.
success_measure: 40% of users record a second take and 25% export or keep a preferred take in the same session.
monetization: free — privacy and one-off usefulness are central; a paywall would undermine the trust proposition.
constraints: Never upload audio; explain that metrics are recording guidance rather than health/voice-quality judgments; require mic permission only on record.
why_distinct: It addresses recording comfort and understandable feedback, not audio editing, AI enhancement, or clinical voice analysis.

title: Family Doodle Relay
user: A parent and child playing remotely who want a calm, reasonably priced cooperative game with no ads, data harvesting, or recurring pressure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent asks for a sane casual remote co-op mobile game for a father and ten-year-old, citing dark patterns, data harvesting, recurring fees, and misleading reviews.
A requester asks for real-time collaborative drawing with instant sync, touch support, and user-join indicators, showing a parallel need for simple shared-canvas interaction.

recurrence: A specific family co-op request and a separate request for immediate multiplayer drawing both support a small, shared-creation interaction rather than another content-heavy game.
current_workaround: Try ad-filled mobile games, screen-share a drawing app, or use generic calls plus a whiteboard.
incumbents_and_gap: Skribbl, Gartic Phone, Roblox, and commercial co-op games are either public/social, competitive, content-heavy, or monetised through ads. The gap is a private two-person relay designed for a child and trusted adult.
smallest_useful_product: A two-person web room with one private invite code, alternating 45-second draw/guess/add-a-detail rounds, large touch controls, no chat with strangers, and an end-of-session locally downloadable strip. Non-goals: public lobbies, ads, profiles, text chat, or user-generated content discovery.
success_measure: 60% of created rooms connect a second player and complete four rounds; fewer than 2% of rooms need reconnect help.
monetization: one-time — a small family-safe product should not depend on behavioural advertising or recurring extraction.
constraints: Use ephemeral rooms, collect no child profiles, add a host-controlled disconnect, keep invite codes unguessable, and follow child-privacy requirements for any future analytics.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately private cooperative creation ritual, not a public drawing-game clone or a social network for children.
